title: Global Current Practice Patterns for the Management of Open Globe Injuries
condition_or_topic: Global management practices for open globe injuries (OGI)
clinical_background: Ocular trauma is a leading cause of blindness in one eye in the United States of America (USA). Worldwide, nearly 55 million eye injuries occur per year, with reduced visual acuity in 19 million people and blindness in 1.6 million people. The estimated global incidence of OGI is 3.5 per 100,000 people, although limited data from low- and middle-income countries suggest that its true prevalence may be underestimated. Management differs across regions and, more often, institutions. The Birmingham Eye Trauma Terminology System (BETTS), developed in 1996, standardizes injury classification but does not address management. The American Academy of Ophthalmology Preferred Practice Patterns (PPP) do not cover OGI, and disagreements about treatment and standards of care persist. Variation in practice is not necessarily harmful, but unevaluated differences could affect access to care, patient outcomes and resource use.
objectives: Describe current institutional approaches to managing OGI worldwide.
Identify areas of variation in OGI management and seek broadly accepted principles for its care.
study_design: Cross-sectional international online survey of institutional practices for managing open globe injuries. The survey was conducted through Qualtrics from August 13, 2020, to January 8, 2021. Invited ophthalmic trauma specialists were asked to report their institutions’ practices rather than their personal preferences.

population.description: Ophthalmic trauma specialists representing eye trauma institutions worldwide. Experts at 42 institutions were invited; 36 completed the survey, and responses from 33 institutions were included in the analysis.
inclusion_criteria: Institutions treating >12 OGI per year, as determined from survey responses.
Invited specialists were members or affiliates of APOTS or ASOT.
exclusion_criteria: Institutions with low trauma volume (<1 OGI per month).
population.care_setting: Eye trauma centers and emergency departments worldwide.

interventions: Surveyed institutional practices concerning antibiotic and steroid use before, during, and after open globe injury repair.
Surveyed surgical decisions, imaging protocols, and hospital admission practices for open globe injuries.
comparators: Management practices at USA versus non-USA institutions.
Intraoperative antibiotic use and anesthesia practices across injury zones.
statistical_methods: Data were analyzed with Excel and R. Fisher exact and χ2 tests compared the proportions of experts selecting management approaches when applicable. P values of <.05 were considered significant. Unless otherwise specified, proportions used all responding experts as the denominator. For numerical responses given as a range, the mean of the range was used; means were reported with SD.
interpretation: The survey found substantial variation across institutions in OGI care before, during, and after repair. Differences involved antibiotic and steroid use, operative timing and procedures, imaging, trainee participation, and admission practices. Experts tended to use intracameral antibiotics for more anterior injuries and intravitreal antibiotics for more posterior injuries, but the effectiveness of these approaches by injury location remains insufficiently studied. IV moxifloxacin was the most frequently reported preoperative systemic regimen, although its effectiveness relative to regimens examined in randomized trials is unknown. USA and non-USA centers differed significantly in who performed repairs (P < .01), the urgency of IOFB removal (P < .01), and consideration of enucleation or evisceration after NLP (P = .04). The authors consider expert, evidence-based guidance a possible way to reduce unwarranted variation and potentially improve visual outcomes.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Earlier work had identified controversy in ophthalmic trauma care and variation in visual acuity and endophthalmitis after OGI repair. For infection prevention, North and Gardiner recommended beginning 48 hours of IV broad-spectrum treatment with agents such as vancomycin and ceftazidime at presentation, without postponing surgery, and continuing the IV treatment after closure for up to 48 hours. A separate investigation reported a 0.9% endophthalmitis rate with IV cefepime and vancomycin. In a randomized trial, oral ciprofloxacin plus IV cefazolin and oral ciprofloxacin plus oral cefuroxime did not differ significantly in endophthalmitis prevention; the reported rates were 2%-3%, compared with 0.9% in the cefepime and vancomycin investigation. Most preoperative regimens reported in the present survey differed from those studied regimens. Prior studies found that intraocular antibiotics could reach therapeutic ocular concentrations and significantly lower endophthalmitis risk without significantly improving final visual acuity. A randomized trial found intraoperative intravitreal clindamycin and gentamicin effective for preventing endophthalmitis; vancomycin and ceftazidime had also been proposed to avoid aminoglycoside-associated retinotoxicity. Other groups found intraoperative antibiotics advantageous only for injuries at highest risk, such as those involving IOFB. Another study reported no difference in posttraumatic endophthalmitis or visual acuity between postoperative IV vancomycin plus ceftazidime and oral ciprofloxacin, with an endophthalmitis rate of approximately 2.1%. A retrospective study published in 2009 reported 0.9% posttraumatic endophthalmitis over 7 years under one institution's standardized perioperative regimen; the authors suggest this may support standardized protocols. Previous studies associated repair delayed more than 24 hours with a significantly higher endophthalmitis rate and suggested that even 12 hours of delay may raise risk. Blanch and associates reported in 2019 that visual acuity decreased for every 24 hours of repair delay; other studies supported this association, although a smaller data set disputed it. Increased morbidity and mortality with out-of-hours surgery has been reported in other specialties, but the authors note no comparable ophthalmology study. Prior research indicates that primary enucleation to prevent sympathetic ophthalmia may often be unnecessary and that evisceration may be preferable. Earlier CT studies reported variable benefits: CT may help detect occult OGI, IOFB, orbital fractures, and vitreous hemorrhage, but its contribution to initial management is unclear. A separate United Kingdom survey found that more than 42.5% of residents had not repaired a traumatic corneal laceration and 60.0% had not repaired an OGI; another investigation found that only 64.5% of surveyed USA residents felt comfortable managing orbital trauma.
clinical_implications: Traumatic endophthalmitis can cause irreversible visual loss; the unresolved choice of antibiotic regimen and route has implications for infection prevention and visual outcomes.

Unexamined differences in care may contribute to unequal access, divergent patient outcomes, and inefficient resource use, although variation can also be justified when approaches provide equivalent benefit.
Delaying OGI repair may increase infection risk and worsen vision, while the balance between that risk and potential risks of out-of-hours surgery remains uncertain in ophthalmology.
Sympathetic ophthalmia may affect both the injured and contralateral eye, but the benefit of removing an eye with NLP to prevent it has not been established.
The value of CT findings for initial OGI decisions remains uncertain; imaging choices may also reflect differences in CT availability.
practice_implications: Develop evidence-based international guidance for OGI care to help replace subjective, ad hoc decisions and reduce unnecessary variation.
Consolidate research findings into high-level guidance on antibiotic treatment and provide educational initiatives for eye care physicians worldwide.
Develop evidence-based guidance on CT use during initial OGI evaluation, with attention to high-value care and cost-effectiveness, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.
limitations: The sample was limited, and some geographic regions were underrepresented or absent; Australia and Europe each contributed only 1 included response.
The survey may not have reached, or received responses from, every highest-volume center, limiting generalizability.
Selecting invitees who were members or affiliates of ASOT and APOTS may have introduced selection bias.
Administration only in English may have led experts whose first language was not English to misinterpret questions.

Despite instructions to report institutional practices, personal practice patterns and recall bias may have affected responses. Variation among physicians within a center may not be fully represented.
strengths: The authors describe the study as a comprehensive assessment of current OGI management at high-volume centers in a cohort of a size not previously studied.
Differences among responses make persistent areas of controversy visible.
open_questions: Which antibiotic regimens and administration routes best prevent infection and preserve vision after OGI, including whether preoperative topical antibiotics provide benefits that outweigh potential harms?
How effective are different intraoperative antibiotic routes for injuries in different zones?
How urgently must OGI be repaired and IOFB removed to minimize patient risk?
Does the risk of sympathetic ophthalmia justify removing an injured eye, and which procedure is preferable when removal is considered?
What is the definitive role of CT and other imaging in initial OGI evaluation?
How does earlier trainee participation in OGI evaluation and repair affect patient outcomes and trainee preparedness?
future_directions: Investigate antibiotic regimens and routes further to address discrepancies between published evidence and practice, reduce infection risk, and improve visual outcomes.
Determine the urgency of OGI repair and IOFB removal needed to minimize patient risk.
Conduct randomized, controlled investigations of sympathetic ophthalmia risk, preservation of native tissue, and the optimal surgical approach.
Clarify the role and value of imaging in OGI evaluation.
Study how early resident and trainee involvement affects clinical outcomes and preparedness so training can be improved while maintaining standards of care.

scales_and_classifications.description: A system for classifying open and closed globe injuries; it does not provide management guidance.

scales_and_classifications.name: Zone 1 OGI
scales_and_classifications.description: Open globe injuries involving the cornea and limbus.

scales_and_classifications.description: Open globe injuries involving anterior sclera up to 5 mm beyond the limbus.

main_findings.description: The survey received responses from 36 of 42 invited institutions; 33 institutions met the trauma-volume criterion for analysis.
main_findings.context: The remaining invitations comprised 5 (11.9) without a response, 1 (2.4) incomplete response, and 3 (7.1) institutions excluded for low trauma volume.

main_findings.description: Included institutions were distributed across six geographic regions.
main_findings.value: North America: 12 (36.4); Asia: 12 (36.4); South America: 4 (12.1); Africa: 3 (9.1); Europe: 1 (3.0); Australia: 1 (3.0)
main_findings.context: Regional proportions refer to the 33 included institutions.

main_findings.description: Respondents described their clinical experience and their institutions’ ophthalmic trauma resources.
main_findings.value: Years practicing after residency: 14.27 ± 7.46; designated trauma center: 17 (51.5); eye-specific emergency department: 19 (57.6); continuous ophthalmology coverage: 25 (75.8); on-call ophthalmologist available within 1 hour when continuous coverage was absent: 8 (100.0)
main_findings.context: Table 1 reports years practicing after residency as 14.3 ± 7.5. The on-call figure pertains to the 8 institutions without continuous ophthalmology coverage.

main_findings.description: Most institutions routinely gave systemic antibiotics before open globe injury repair, whereas fewer routinely gave topical antibiotics.
main_findings.value: Systemic: 25 (75.8); topical: 10 (30.3)
main_findings.context: Both practices could be reported by the same institution; percentages use the 33 included institutions.

main_findings.description: Reported oral systemic antibiotic choices before repair varied among institutions.
main_findings.value: Ciprofloxacin: 4 (12.1); Moxifloxacin: 3 (9.1)
main_findings.context: These are preoperative oral regimens.

main_findings.description: Reported intravenous systemic antibiotic choices before repair varied; Moxifloxacin was the most frequently reported individual regimen.
main_findings.value: Moxifloxacin: 6 (18.2); Ceftazidime and vancomycin: 2 (6.1); Ceftriaxone and gentamicin: 2 (6.1); Ceftriaxone: 2 (6.1); Ciprofloxacin: 2 (6.1); Levofloxacin: 2 (6.1); Ceftriaxone and metronidazole: 1 (3.0); Cefazolin and gentamicin: 1 (3.0); Cefazolin and levofloxacin: 1 (3.0); Moxifloxacin and vancomycin: 1 (3.0)
main_findings.context: These are preoperative intravenous regimens.

main_findings.description: Institutional approaches to preoperative systemic antibiotics in children were not uniform.
main_findings.value: No standard: 2 (6.1); same as in adults: 8 (24.2); different from adults: 13 (39.4); no information: 10 (30.3)
main_findings.context: Examples of pediatric regimens included intravenous ceftazidime and vancomycin and intravenous ceftriaxone.

main_findings.description: Preoperative topical antibiotic selections differed among the institutions using this approach.
main_findings.value: Moxifloxacin: 6 (18.2); Ofloxacin: 1 (3.0); Fortified tobramycin and vancomycin: 1 (3.0); Ciprofloxacin and chloramphenicol: 1 (3.0); Moxifloxacin and amikacin: 1 (3.0)
main_findings.context: The listed choices concern antibiotic administration before repair.

main_findings.description: Ophthalmic antibiotics were administered during repair at similar frequencies for zone 1 and zones 2 and 3; the difference was not statistically significant.
main_findings.context: The comparison used a χ2 test. Experts could select more than 1 route for each zone; intraoperative treatment could accompany preoperative antibiotics.

main_findings.description: Intracameral antibiotic administration was reported more often for zone 1 than for zones 2 and 3.
main_findings.context: Intracameral choices in zone 1 were Moxifloxacin 8 (24.2), Cephalosporin 6 (18.2), and Vancomycin 3 (9.1); in zones 2 and 3 they were Moxifloxacin 6 (18.2), Cephalosporin 2 (6.1), and Vancomycin 1 (3.0).

main_findings.description: Intravitreal antibiotic administration was reported less often for zone 1 than for zones 2 and 3.
main_findings.context: Intravitreal choices in zone 1 were Moxifloxacin 1 (3.0), Vancomycin 6 (18.2), Cephalosporin 5 (15.2), and Aminoglycoside 0 (0.0); in zones 2 and 3 they were Moxifloxacin 0 (0.0), Vancomycin 7 (21.2), Cephalosporin 7 (21.2), and Aminoglycoside 1 (3.0).

main_findings.description: Subconjunctival and other intraoperative antibiotic routes were also reported for each injury-zone grouping.
main_findings.value: Subconjunctival, zone 1: 4 (12.1); subconjunctival, zones 2 and 3: 4 (12.1); other route, zone 1: 2 (6.1); other route, zones 2 and 3: 2 (6.1)
main_findings.context: Other routes included topical administration; selection could depend on the affected ocular structure or the surgeon.

main_findings.description: Systemic antibiotic use after repair was less frequent than before repair; every included institution routinely used postoperative topical antibiotics.
main_findings.value: Postoperative systemic: 23 (69.7); preoperative systemic: 25 (75.8); postoperative topical: 33 (100.0); postoperative systemic regimen duration: 4.7 ± 4.0 days
main_findings.context: The duration applies to systemic antibiotic regimens after repair.

main_findings.description: Institutions reported several systemic antibiotic regimens after repair.
main_findings.value: Oral ciprofloxacin: 9 (27.3); Oral moxifloxacin: 5 (15.2); Oral levofloxacin: 3 (9.1); Oral amoxicillin clavulanate: 1 (3.0); Oral fluoroquinolone (unspecified): 1 (3.0); IV ceftriaxone: 1 (3.0); IV ceftriaxone, IV gentamicin, and oral moxifloxacin: 1 (3.0)
main_findings.context: The institution reporting the final regimen also used cefotaxime instead of ceftriaxone in some circumstances.

main_findings.description: Postoperative topical antibiotic selection varied, although Moxifloxacin was the most commonly listed choice.
main_findings.value: Moxifloxacin: 19 (57.6); Ofloxacin: 6 (18.2); Chloramphenicol: 2 (6.1); Ciprofloxacin: 1 (3.0); Ciprofloxacin, tobramycin: 1 (3.0); Fortified cefazolin: 1 (3.0); Fortified gentamicin: 1 (3.0); Gatifloxacin: 1 (3.0); Levofloxacin: 1 (3.0); Moxifloxacin, amikacin: 1 (3.0); Ofloxacin, tobramycin, moxifloxacin: 1 (3.0); Polytrim: 1 (3.0); Unspecified quinolones: 1 (3.0); Vancomycin, cefuroxime: 1 (3.0)
main_findings.context: These are reported topical choices after repair.

main_findings.description: Most institutions routinely prescribed topical steroids after repair.
main_findings.value: Topical steroids: 29 (87.9); Prednisolone: 28 (84.8); Difluprednate: 4 (12.1); duration: 26.9 ± 12.9 days
main_findings.context: Duration includes tapering; respondents could select more than 1 steroid.

main_findings.description: Residents commonly conducted initial assessments at institutions with trainees.
main_findings.value: Resident: 24 (77.4) of 31; fellow: 6 (19.4) of 31; attending: 11 (33.3) of 33
main_findings.context: Responses could include more than 1 physician level. Among the 24 institutions where residents assessed suspected injuries, they began at PGY2 in 18 (75.0), PGY3 in 5 (20.8), and PGY4 in 1 (4.2).

main_findings.description: Institutions differed on when to repair an open globe injury presenting after hours.
main_findings.value: As soon as possible, including overnight: 13 (39.4); first case next day: 12 (36.4); first available operating-room space next day: 8 (24.2)
main_findings.context: Timing is relative to presentation.

main_findings.description: Preferred timing for removal of an intraocular foreign body also differed among institutions.
main_findings.value: As soon as possible, including overnight: 12 (36.4); first case next day: 8 (24.2); first available operating-room space next day: 7 (21.2); dependent on foreign-body type: 6 (18.2)
main_findings.context: Respondents in the last group identified copper, organic material, and iron as requiring emergent removal.

main_findings.description: Residents participated in supervised repairs at many institutions with trainees.
main_findings.value: Resident with direct supervision: 19 (61.3) of 31; fellow: 2 (6.5) of 31; attending: 12 (36.4) of 33
main_findings.context: Among 19 institutions allowing supervised resident repair, the reported starting levels were PGY2: 2 (10.5), PGY3: 11 (57.9), and PGY4: 5 (26.3); 1 institution did not specify a starting year.

main_findings.description: Routine CT imaging for every presenting open globe injury was used by nearly half of institutions; others obtained CT when an intraocular foreign body or orbital fracture was suspected.
main_findings.value: CT for all presenting injuries: 16 (48.5); CT when an intraocular foreign body or orbital fracture was suspected: 15 (45.5)
main_findings.context: Orbital CT with fine cuts accounted for 45.5% of CT-type selections.

main_findings.description: Institutions were divided on obtaining preoperative B-scan ultrasonography when the posterior segment could not be viewed.
main_findings.value: Obtained: 15 (45.5); not obtained: 18 (54.5)
main_findings.context: The assessment concerns imaging before open globe repair.

main_findings.description: General anesthesia was selected increasingly often across progressively posterior injury zones, but anesthesia-type distributions did not differ significantly by zone.
main_findings.value: General anesthesia, zone 1: 16 (48.5); zone 2: 18 (54.5); zone 3: 22 (66.7)
main_findings.context: Fisher exact test. Retrobulbar: zone 1 4 (12.1), zone 2 4 (12.1), zone 3 4 (12.1); peribulbar: 12 (36.4), 9 (27.3), 6 (18.2); Subtenon: 0 (0.0), 1 (3.0), 1 (3.0); topical or intracameral: 1 (3.0), 1 (3.0), 0 (0.0). One zone 1 institution using peribulbar anesthesia also used retrobulbar anesthesia.

main_findings.description: For zone 1 injuries involving anterior lens capsule violation and/or visually significant traumatic cataract, cataract removal without intraocular lens placement was the most common reported approach.

subgroup_analyses: The comparison comprised USA institutions, 11 (33.3) of 33, and international institutions, 22 (66.7) of 33. Routine preoperative systemic antibiotics were reported by 10 (90.9) USA versus 15 (68.2) international institutions (P = .22); preoperative topical antibiotics by 1 (9.1) versus 9 (40.9) (P = .11).

Routine intraoperative antibiotics were reported by 6 (54.5) of 11 USA and 12 (54.5) of 22 international institutions (P = 1.00). For zone 1, the corresponding counts were 6 (54.5) versus 12 (54.5) (P = 1.00); for zones 2 and 3, 6 (54.5) versus 11 (50.0) (P = 1.00).

Routine postoperative systemic antibiotics were reported by 7 (63.6) USA versus 16 (72.7) international institutions (P = .70); topical antibiotics by 11 (100.0) versus 22 (100.0) (P = 1.00); and topical steroids by 9 (81.8) versus 20 (90.9) (P = .59). Mean ± SD topical steroid duration was 38.9 ± 16.1 days in USA centers and 22.7 ± 8.5 days in international centers.

Routine discharge after closure was reported by 8 (72.7) USA versus 7 (31.8) international centers (P = .06); routine hospital admission by 3 (27.3) versus 15 (68.2) (P = .06). Mean ± SD admission length was 44.0 ± 18.3 hours versus 56.2 ± 38.7 hours, respectively.

Not considering enucleation or evisceration for no light perception after injury was reported by 4 (36.4) USA versus 14 (63.6) international centers (P = .04). Enucleation was reported by 3 (27.3) versus 3 (13.6); evisceration by 1 (9.1) versus 5 (22.7); and a case- or surgeon-dependent choice by 3 (27.3) versus 0 (0.0), respectively.

Preferred repair timing did not differ significantly between USA and international institutions (P = .81): immediate repair, including overnight, 4 (36.4) versus 9 (40.9); first case next day, 5 (45.5) versus 7 (31.8); first available operating-room space next day, 2 (18.2) versus 6 (27.3).

Initial evaluation by residents was reported by 11 (100.0) of 11 USA versus 13 (65.0) of 20 international institutions with trainees; evaluation by fellows by 1 (9.1) of 11 versus 5 (25.0) of 20; and evaluation by attendings by 2 (18.2) of 11 versus 9 (40.9) of 22. Among institutions where residents evaluated injuries, starting at PGY2 was reported by 11 (100.0) USA versus 7 (53.8) international centers, PGY3 by 0 (0.0) versus 5 (38.5), and PGY4 by 0 (0.0) versus 1 (7.7); the comparison of starting levels had P = .02.

The physician levels performing repairs differed significantly between USA and international centers (P < .01). Supervised residents performed repairs at 11 (100.0) of 11 USA versus 8 (40.0) of 20 international centers with trainees; fellows at 0 (0.0) versus 2 (10.0); and attendings at 0 (0.0) of 11 versus 12 (54.5) of 22. Among centers reporting when supervised resident repair began, PGY2 was reported by 2 (18.2) USA versus 0 (0.0) international centers, PGY3 by 6 (54.5) versus 5 (62.5), and PGY4 by 3 (27.3) versus 2 (25.0); the starting-level comparison had P = .79.

Preferred timing of intraocular foreign-body removal differed significantly between USA and international centers (P < .01). Removal as soon as possible, including overnight, was selected by 9 (81.8) versus 3 (13.6); first case next day by 1 (9.1) versus 7 (31.8); first available operating-room space next day by 0 (0.0) versus 7 (31.8); and timing dependent on the foreign-body type by 1 (9.1) versus 5 (22.7).

For zone 1 lens capsule violation or traumatic cataract, cataract removal alone was reported by 6 (54.5) USA versus 17 (77.3) international centers (P = .24); removal with IOL placement by 0 (0.0) versus 5 (22.7) (P = .14); and considering both approaches by 0 (0.0) versus 4 (18.2) (P = .28).

For zone 2 initial repairs, prophylactic laser photocoagulation was reported by 0 (0.0) USA versus 3 (13.6) international centers (P = .53), and cryopexy by 0 (0.0) versus 3 (13.6) (P = .53). For zone 3, prophylactic scleral buckle was reported by 0 (0.0) versus 4 (18.2) (P = .28).

Vitrectomy timing after repair did not differ significantly between USA and international centers (P = .13): within 4 days, 0 (0.0) versus 7 (31.8); 4-7 days, 2 (18.2) versus 4 (18.2); ≥7 days, 6 (54.5) versus 9 (40.9); and timing dependent on visualization and retinal specialists’ opinion, 3 (27.3) versus 2 (9.1).

For retinal detachment with an opaque cornea, the USA-versus-international comparison was not statistically significant (P = .11). Observation until corneal clearing was reported by 2 (18.2) versus 12 (54.5); temporary keratoprosthesis and corneal transplant during retinal repair by 5 (45.5) versus 8 (36.4); a decision left to retinal specialists by 2 (18.2) versus 1 (4.5); and a case-dependent decision by 2 (18.2) versus 1 (4.5).

Cyanoacrylate glue use was reported by 10 (90.9) USA versus 15 (68.2) international centers (P = .22). Routine CT for open globe injuries was more frequent at USA centers, 10 (90.9) versus 6 (27.3) (P < .01); CT only for suspected intraocular foreign body and/or orbital fracture was reported by 1 (9.1) versus 14 (63.6), and CT only for other indications by 0 (0.0) versus 2 (9.1).

CT types selected by USA versus international centers were standard head CT, 3 (27.3) versus 5 (22.7); orbital CT, 3 (27.3) versus 9 (40.9); orbital CT with fine cuts, 8 (72.7) versus 12 (54.5); 3-Dimensional CT, 0 (0.0) versus 2 (9.1); and other CT, 1 (9.1) versus 1 (4.5). Centers could select multiple types.

Preoperative B-scan when the posterior segment could not be viewed was reported by 3 (27.3) USA versus 12 (54.5) international centers (P = .27); not obtaining it was reported by 8 (72.7) versus 10 (45.5). Postoperative B-scan timing differed with P = .05: 1 day, 4 (36.4) versus 15 (68.2); 2-3 days, 0 (0.0) versus 2 (9.1); 1 week, 7 (63.6) versus 4 (18.2); and 1 month, 0 (0.0) versus 1 (4.5).

In a geographic description of CT use, all responding African institutions, 3/3 (100%), and 10/12 (83.3%) Asian institutions limited CT to selected indications; 10 of 12 (83.3%) North American and 3 of 4 (75.0%) South American institutions obtained CT for all suspected open globe injuries.
secondary_results: In the authors’ further description of their survey, 19 (57.6%) institutions used only 1 systemic antibiotic before repair; 2 (6.1%) reported intravenous ceftazidime and vancomycin.
Only oral antibiotics after repair were reported by 19 (57.5%) institutions. Among those 19 institutions, 8 (42.1%) routinely discharged patients without admission after closure.

The authors described 20 (60.6%) institutions as waiting until morning to repair an injury presenting overnight. For cases involving an intraocular foreign body, 15 (45.5%) followed a next-day approach, while 6 (18.2%) made urgency dependent on foreign-body characteristics.

main_conclusion: Preferred approaches to open globe injury management vary substantially across institutions. The authors call for international, evidence-based guidance to support consistently high standards of care.
narrative_summary: This cross-sectional survey examined institutional approaches to open globe injuries at high-volume ophthalmic trauma centers worldwide. Representatives of 36 of 42 invited institutions responded, and 33 met the trauma-volume criterion for analysis. Questions addressed antimicrobial and steroid use, imaging, operative decisions, trainee participation, and disposition after repair. Before surgery, 25 (75.8%) institutions routinely administered systemic antibiotics and 10 (30.3%) used topical antibiotics. Intraoperative ophthalmic antibiotics were reported for zone 1 injuries by 18 (54.5%) institutions and for zone 2 and 3 injuries by 17 (51.5%); the difference was not significant (P = .81). After repair, 23 (69.7%) routinely used systemic antibiotics, all 33 (100.0%) used topical antibiotics, and 29 (87.9%) used topical steroids. Repair timing, CT and B-scan practices, anesthesia, subsequent procedures, and admission policies also varied. Hospital admission after primary closure was routine at 18 (54.5%) institutions. Compared with international centers, USA centers differed significantly in the level of clinician performing repair (P < .01), preferred urgency of intraocular foreign body removal (P < .01), and routine CT use (P < .01). The survey describes practice preferences, not comparative patient outcomes or the effectiveness of particular regimens. Its limited and geographically uneven sample, potential selection and recall biases, English-only administration, and possible within-institution variation restrict interpretation. The authors identify a need for further investigation and evidence-based international guidance.

document_sections.heading: PURPOSE
document_sections.content: The study sought to describe current worldwide approaches to managing open globe injuries and identify where practice differs.

document_sections.heading: DESIGN
document_sections.content: The authors conducted a cross-sectional survey.

document_sections.heading: METHODS
document_sections.content: From August 2020 to January 2021, an online survey gathered institutional practices from eye trauma centers and emergency departments worldwide that managed ≥1 open globe injury per month. Questions addressed antibiotics, steroids, procedures, imaging, and admission.

document_sections.heading: RESULTS
document_sections.content: Representatives of 36 of 42 institutions responded (85.7%); 33 (78.6%) met the trauma-volume criterion. Included institutions were in North America (n=12, 36.4%), Asia (n=12, 36.4%), South America (n=4, 12.1%), Africa (n=3, 9.1%), Europe (n=1, 3.0%), and Australia (n=1, 3.0%). Preoperative systemic antibiotics were routine at 75.8% (n = 25/33) of institutions, compared with preoperative topical antibiotics at 30.3% (n = 10/33). Intraoperative ophthalmic antibiotics were used by 54.5% (n = 18/33). Postoperative systemic antibiotics were routine at n = 23 [69.7%] and topical steroids at n = 29 [87.9%], although drug choices differed. Residents helped perform repairs at 19 centers (61.3% of the 31 with trainees). Routine admission for observation after repair occurred at 54.5% (n = 18/33) of locations; other institutions discharged patients.

document_sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
document_sections.content: Preferred approaches to open globe injury differ substantially. The authors call for evidence-based international treatment guidelines to support consistently high standards of care.

Ocular trauma is a major cause of blindness in one eye in the USA. Worldwide, nearly 55 million eye injuries occur each year, with reduced visual acuity in 19 million people and blindness in 1.6 million. Estimated open globe injury incidence is 3.5 per 100,000 people. Male sex, industrial work, and lower socioeconomic status have been linked to greater risk of traumatic eye injury. Estimates from low- and middle-income countries are scarce, so the true prevalence of open globe injury is thought to be underestimated. Management currently follows regional or, more often, institutional guidance. Developed in 1996, the internationally accepted Birmingham Eye Trauma Terminology System (BETTS) standardized classification of open and closed globe injuries, but its injury definitions have limited scope and it provides no management framework. The American Academy of Ophthalmology has issued Preferred Practice Patterns (PPP) for common eye diseases, but these do not address common trauma such as open globe injury. Despite institutional and collaborative assessments of treatments, disputes about practice and standards remain. Differences in care are not necessarily harmful: individualized treatment can foster new approaches and better responses. Nevertheless, differing practices need evaluation to establish comparable patient benefit or another justification. Unexamined variation could contribute to unequal access, different outcomes, and inefficient resource use. The authors therefore surveyed institutions internationally to summarize preferred management, pursue broadly accepted principles, and locate worldwide variation.

document_sections.heading: METHODS
document_sections.content: The methods comprise survey development, distribution, ethics review, and analysis of institutional responses.

document_sections.heading: SURVEY DEVELOPMENT
document_sections.content: The Qualtrics (SAP) survey ran from August 13, 2020, to January 8, 2021. Questions drew on relevant PPP guidance and practices at the Wilmer Eye Institute of the Johns Hopkins Hospital, Wills Eye Hospital, Bascom Palmer Eye Institute, and University Hospitals Birmingham. Cornea, retina, and other trauma experts affiliated with the American Society for Ophthalmic Trauma (ASOT), the International Globe and Adnexal Trauma Epidemiology Study (IGATES), and the Asia Pacific Ophthalmic Trauma Society (APOTS) reviewed and refined the questions. The final instrument had 123 questions, including 26 free-text items; 58 concerned open globe injury management or institutional characteristics. Zone 1 encompassed the cornea and limbus; zone 2 encompassed anterior sclera up to 5 mm beyond the limbus; zone 3 encompassed sclera more than 5 mm behind the limbus.

document_sections.heading: SURVEY DISTRIBUTION
document_sections.content: Ophthalmologists specializing in trauma received email invitations and up to 3 follow-up messages per expert or location. They were asked to report institutional practice rather than personal preference. Invitees belonged to or were affiliated with APOTS or ASOT. The final analysis included institutions reporting >12 open globe injuries per year.

document_sections.heading: ETHICAL APPROVAL
document_sections.content: The Johns Hopkins School of Medicine Institutional Review Board considered the study exempt because participant risk was minimal. No patient information was collected; the work complied with Maryland law and the Declaration of Helsinki, and respondents consented.

document_sections.heading: DATA ANALYSIS
document_sections.content: Analyses used Excel (Microsoft, Inc.) and R (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, 2017). Fisher exact and χ2 tests compared response proportions where applicable; P values <.05 were considered significant. Unless specified otherwise, percentages used all responding experts as the denominator. For a reported numerical range, such as 7-10 days, the investigators analyzed its mean. Means were presented with SD. Preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative refer to timing relative to globe repair unless otherwise stated.

document_sections.heading: RESULTS
document_sections.content: The results describe respondents, medication practices, surgical and imaging protocols, and comparisons between USA and non-USA centers.

document_sections.heading: SUMMARY OF RESPONDENTS
document_sections.content: Experts at 42 institutions received the survey; 36 completed it, giving a response rate of 85.7%. Three centers, one each in North America, Asia, and Europe, were excluded because they managed <1 open globe injury per month. Continuous in-house ophthalmology coverage was available to n = 25 [75.8%] of included centers; all 8 (100.0%) without it had an on-call ophthalmologist available within 1 hour. Experts had practiced for a mean of 14.27 ± 7.46 years after residency. The supplemental table describes annual injury volumes.

document_sections.content: This table summarizes invitation outcomes, the geographic distribution and experience of included respondents, and institutional trauma and ophthalmology-service capabilities.

document_sections.heading: ANTIBIOTIC AND STEROID MANAGEMENT PARADIGMS FOR OGI
document_sections.content: Preoperative systemic antibiotics were routinely given by n = 25 [75.8%] of experts. IV moxifloxacin was the most frequent systemic choice, reported by 6 experts (18.2%). Pediatric approaches matched adult regimens for 8 experts (24.2%) and included IV ceftazidime and vancomycin or IV ceftriaxone; 2 experts (6.1%) had no pediatric systemic-antibiotic standard. Before adult repair, 10 experts (30.3%) routinely used topical antibiotics, alone or with systemic treatment, and 6 (18.2%) favored topical moxifloxacin. Intraoperative ophthalmic antibiotics were less common than preoperative antibiotics (n = 18 [54.5%] vs n = 25 [75.8%]); the practices could overlap. Intraocular antibiotics were used for zone 1 by 54.5% (n = 18/33) and for zones 2 and 3 by 51.5% (n = 17/33), without a significant difference (P = .81 by χ2 test). Multiple administration routes could be selected. For zone 1, intracameral use was reported by 42.4% (n = 14/33) and intravitreal use by 18.2% (n = 6/33); for zones 2 and 3, 9 experts (27.3%) used intravitreal and 8 (24.2%) intracameral antibiotics. For each zone grouping, 4 experts (12.1%) used subconjunctival antibiotics during repair, potentially alongside intraocular treatment. Postoperative systemic antibiotics were less frequent than preoperative systemic antibiotics (n = 23 [69.7%] vs n = 25 [75.8%]); postoperative systemic courses averaged 4.7 ± 4.0 days. Every expert routinely used topical antibiotics after repair (n = 33 [100.0%]). Postoperative topical steroids were reported by n = 29 [87.9%], commonly prednisolone (n = 28 [84.8%]) or difluprednate (n = 4 [12.1%]); treatment, including tapering, averaged 26.9 ± 12.9 days.

document_sections.heading: SURGICAL PROTOCOLS FOR OGI REPAIRS
document_sections.content: Surgical approaches differed among experts, institutions, and regions. Two institutions had no residents, fellows, or trainees. At 24 institutions (77.4% of the 31 with residents or trainees), residents generally performed the first assessment of suspected injury. Among those 24, evaluation began in the first ophthalmology training year at 75.0% (18/24), the second at 20.8% (5/24), and the third at 4.2% (1/24). For repair, 13 experts (39.4%) preferred surgery as soon as possible, including overnight; after-hours presentations were instead scheduled as the first case next day by 12 (36.4%) or in the first available operating-room slot next day by 8 (24.2%). For suspected intraocular foreign body, 6 experts (18.2%) based removal urgency on its material and identified copper, organic material, and iron as emergent. Among experts not using its nature to set urgency, 12 (36.4%) favored surgery as soon as possible, 8 (24.2%) the first case next day, and 7 (21.2%) the first available slot next day. Residents could repair open globes under direct supervision at 19 centers (61.3% of the 31 with residents or trainees), while fellows could assist at 2 (6.5% of the 31); attending physicians performed repair at 12 centers (36.4% of all respondents). Among centers permitting resident surgery, 11 (57.9%) began supervised repair in the second ophthalmology year. CT was routine for every presenting injury at 16 centers (48.5%), whereas 15 (45.5%) obtained it for suspected intraocular foreign body or orbital fracture. When CT was performed, fine-cut orbital CT was the most frequent selection (45.5% of selections). With no posterior view, 15 experts (45.5%) routinely obtained preoperative B-scan ultrasonography and 18 (54.5%) did not. For zone 1 repair, general (n = 16 [48.5%]), peribulbar (n = 12 [36.4%]), and retrobulbar (n = 4 [12.1%]) anesthesia predominated. General anesthesia was more frequent for zone 2 (n = 18 [54.5%]) and zone 3 (n = 22 [66.7%]); anesthesia type did not differ significantly by zone (P = .73, Fisher exact test). For zone 1 anterior lens capsule injury and/or a visually significant traumatic cataract treated at initial repair, 23 experts (69.7%) removed the cataract without lens implantation and 5 (15.2%) also implanted an intraocular lens. At initial zone 2 repair, prophylactic laser photocoagulation and cryopexy were each reported by n = 3 [9.1%]; at zone 3 repair, n = 4 [12.1%] routinely placed a prophylactic scleral buckle. Cyanoacrylate glue was used when appropriate by n = 25 [75.8%]. When vitrectomy was indicated, n = 15/33 (45.5%) favored ≥7 days after initial repair, n = 7 [21.2%] favored within 4 days, and n = 6 [18.2%] favored 4 to 7 days. For suspected retinal detachment obscured by the cornea, 14 experts (42.4%) waited for corneal clearing and 13 (39.4%) used a temporary keratoprosthesis and corneal transplant during retinal surgery. Postoperative B-scan was preferred on day 1 by 19 (57.6%) and at 1 week by 11 (33.3%). Following injury and repair with no light perception, 18.2% (n = 6/33) considered enucleation and 18.2% (n = 6/33) considered evisceration. After primary closure, n = 18 [54.5%] routinely admitted patients for an average of 54.3 ± 36.1 hours; n = 15 [45.5%] discharged them after surgery.

document_sections.heading: OGI MANAGEMENT IN USA VS. NON-USA CENTERS
document_sections.content: Table 4 compares institutional management inside and outside the USA. The level of physician performing repair differed significantly (P < .01, Fisher exact test): directly supervised residents performed repairs at all USA centers, 100.0% (n = 11), versus 40.0% of non-USA centers (n = 8/20). For eyes with no light perception after injury, USA experts were more likely than non-USA experts to consider enucleation (n = 3 [27.3%]), evisceration (n = 1 [9.1%]), or either depending on the case or surgeon (n = 3 [27.3%]); the geographic difference was significant (P = .04, Fisher exact test).

document_sections.heading: DISCUSSION
document_sections.content: The survey documents differences throughout preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative open globe injury care, including prophylactic medications and procedures. Earlier investigations reported differences in visual acuity and endophthalmitis after repair; the authors suggest expert consensus could reduce unwarranted practice variation and possibly variation in visual outcomes. Antibiotic treatment aims in part to avert traumatic endophthalmitis and potentially irreversible visual loss. In this setting, infection is most commonly attributed to Bacillus species and Staphylococcus epidermidis, but preferred antibiotic agents and routes differ. North and Gardiner recommended starting 48 hours of broad-spectrum IV therapy at presentation, for example vancomycin and ceftazidime, without postponing surgery. Another investigation reported prevention with IV cefepime plus vancomycin and an endophthalmitis rate of 0.9%. A separate randomized trial found no significant prevention difference between oral ciprofloxacin with IV cefazolin and oral ciprofloxacin with oral cefuroxime; its endophthalmitis rates were 2%-3%, versus 0.9% reported with IV vancomycin and cefepime. In the present survey, 75.8% (n = 25/33) gave preoperative systemic antibiotics, but most regimens differed from those trials. Nineteen (57.6%) used only 1 systemic agent before surgery, and 2 experts (6.1%) used IV ceftazidime with vancomycin. IV moxifloxacin was the most common regimen observed. The authors note that IV delivery avoids oral-treatment effects such as nausea when eating or drinking is restricted and that moxifloxacin penetrates the blood-retinal barrier better than vancomycin; its comparative effectiveness against regimens studied in randomized trials remains unknown. Preoperative topical-antibiotic benefits and harms have received little study, and some have hypothesized harm from disturbing ocular contents. Nevertheless, 10 experts (30.3%) routinely used topical antibiotics before primary repair. Earlier studies reported that intraocular antibiotics can reach therapeutic ocular concentrations that systemic dosing may not achieve and significantly lower endophthalmitis risk, without significantly improving final visual acuity. A randomized trial found intraoperative intravitreal clindamycin and gentamicin effective for prevention; vancomycin with ceftazidime has also been proposed to avoid possible aminoglycoside-related retinal toxicity. Survey respondents favored intracameral antibiotics for more anterior injuries and intravitreal antibiotics for posterior injuries, most often moxifloxacin for intracameral and vancomycin for intravitreal delivery. Comparative effectiveness of intraoperative routes by injury site has not been adequately studied; some research groups found an advantage only for highest-risk injuries such as those with an intraocular foreign body. Respondents also lacked agreement about postoperative systemic or topical regimens. North and Gardiner recommended continuing preoperative IV antibiotics for up to 48 hours after closure, an approach requiring admission that may be unavailable to surgeons outside inpatient facilities. A separate study found no difference in posttraumatic endophthalmitis or visual acuity between postoperative IV vancomycin and ceftazidime and oral ciprofloxacin; its endophthalmitis rate was approximately 2.1%. Only oral postoperative antibiotics were reported by n = 19 [57.5%] survey experts; 8 institutions (42.1% of the 19) in that group routinely discharged patients without admission. All surveyed institutions routinely used topical postoperative antibiotics, but selection varied: moxifloxacin was reported by n = 19 [57.6%]. Published approaches also include gatifloxacin, ciprofloxacin, and fortified gentamicin or tobramycin. A retrospective review published in 2009 reported 0.9% posttraumatic endophthalmitis over 7 years under one institution’s protocol of perioperative IV vancomycin and ceftazidime plus postoperative topical prednisolone, moxifloxacin or ofloxacin, and cycloplegics; the authors consider this possible support for standardized care. They call for further study of antibiotic choice and route to reduce infection and improve vision, along with consolidated high-level guidance and education for eye-care physicians worldwide. Repair timing and foreign-body removal also lacked consensus. Prior research associated repair delayed more than 24 hours with significantly more endophthalmitis and suggested that even 12 hours of delay may increase risk. Blanch and associates reported in 2019 that each additional 24 hours before repair corresponded to worse visual acuity, consistent with some studies but disputed by a smaller data set. Surgery outside normal hours has been associated with increased morbidity and mortality in other fields, but no comparable ophthalmology study had been published. In this survey, n = 20 [60.6%] would defer a middle-of-the-night open globe repair until morning; n = 15 [45.5%] did so for foreign-body cases, while 6 experts (18.2%) considered certain materials, including copper or organic material, more urgent. Immediate foreign-body removal, including overnight, was favored by n = 9 [81.8%] USA experts versus n = 3 [13.6%] at international institutions, a significant difference (P < .01). The necessary repair urgency to minimize harm requires further investigation. Sympathetic ophthalmia is a possible severe consequence of injury and can cause granulomatous panuveitis in both the injured and opposite eye. Whether preventive enucleation or evisceration is appropriate remains debated. More USA centers considered these procedures for eyes with no light perception than non-USA centers (P = .04); the authors suggest access to specialized oculoplastic surgeons and high-quality implants as a possible explanation. Earlier studies indicate that primary enucleation to prevent sympathetic ophthalmia may often be unnecessary and that evisceration may be preferable. Randomized controlled investigations are needed to weigh sympathetic ophthalmia risk against preservation of native tissue and determine the best procedure. Imaging also needs clearer evaluation. Prior studies found variable benefit from CT for suspected injury. CT can help screen for occult injury, intraocular foreign body, orbital fracture, and vitreous hemorrhage, especially when a nonspecialist first examines the patient, but whether it materially informs initial management is unclear; imaging findings at presentation may prove more useful after repair. Among surveyed trauma centers, 48.5% (n = 16/33) obtained CT for every suspected injury. Selective CT was used by all responding African centers (n = 3/3 [100%]) and many Asian centers (n = 10/12 [83.3%]); CT for every suspected injury was reported by 10 of 12 (83.3%) North American and 3 of 4 (75.0%) South American centers. Prior CT might help explain why preoperative B-scan with no posterior view was less common in the USA, where n = 3 [27.3%] routinely obtained it, than internationally, where n = 12 [54.5%] did. The authors emphasize evidence-based CT guidance to support cost-effective care, especially in low- and middle-income countries, and note that CT availability may also differ. USA residents participated earlier in evaluation and repair than their international counterparts: surgical participation occurred at 100.0% of USA centers [n=11] versus 40.0% of non-USA centers [n=8]. Another survey found that more than 42.5% of United Kingdom residents had not repaired a traumatic corneal laceration and 60.0% had not repaired an open globe injury. In a separate investigation, only 64.5% of surveyed USA residents said they were comfortable managing orbital trauma. The authors call for research on how early trainee participation affects outcomes and preparedness while maintaining care standards. Limitations include the small sample and underrepresentation or absence of some regions, with only 1 included response each from Australia and Europe. Recruitment may have missed some highest-volume centers, limiting generalizability, and inviting ASOT and APOTS members or affiliates may have introduced selection bias. An English-only survey could have been misinterpreted by experts whose first language was not English. Despite instructions to describe institutional practice, personal habits and recall bias might have influenced responses; variation among clinicians within a center may not be fully represented. As strengths, the authors identify the breadth of this census of high-volume-center practice in a cohort of this size and its demonstration of persistent disagreements. They argue for replacing subjective, ad hoc approaches with evidence-based recommendations to improve visual outcomes and access to high-standard care.
